claims.text: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating on steel has a fine-grained microstructure without pre-formed oxide features.
Pre-annealing at 400–500 °C can produce nanocrystalline oxide pockets at the coating grain boundaries.
The pre-annealing duration can be optimized to make the grain-boundary oxide pockets uniformly distributed.
Grain-boundary oxide pockets act as nucleation sites for a continuous oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
The oxide layer formed during wear is self-healing.
Controlled grain-boundary oxidation limits subsequent uncontrolled oxidation.
The controlled oxide evolution maintains grain-boundary cohesion and prevents localized weakening.
A continuous protective oxide layer reduces abrasive wear and excessive material removal.
Pre-annealing will lower the FeNiCrCoCu coating's wear rate relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Pre-annealing will reduce the coefficient of friction relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Pre-annealing will produce less subsurface damage than the as-deposited condition.
The pre-annealed coating will develop a more stable, uniform, and continuous protective oxide layer during wear.
Evenly distributed oxide features will remain observable at grain boundaries after wear.
The proposed mechanism is effective during sliding wear at 600–700 °C under sustained loads.
Wear behavior in a different high-entropy alloy changes substantially around 650 °C, showing that this temperature range can mark a wear-regime transition.
The optimal pre-annealing duration and temperature are not yet determined.
Beneficial oxidation may be offset by brittleness at the coating–substrate interface.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear-rate and friction reduction, or failure to form a continuous self-healing oxide layer, would falsify the hypothesis.
